AI-powered Bayesian inference: linear regression part

DSC536 project, O’Hagan & Ročková (2025), arXiv:2502.19231

26 November 2026

This document contains the code and a short explanation of every step of the regression part of the project. It runs offline from the files saved in the repository. The only step that needs the internet (asking the LLM for predictions) is shown but not re-run; its outputs are saved in data/llm/.

Question. How is weekly AI use (ai_hours_per_week) related to students’ critical-thinking score (0-100) and CGPA (0-4), and does an LLM-based prior, built as in O’Hagan & Ročková (2025), improve the inference when only a few labelled students are available?

Main points: the data are clean (no missing values, duplicates or impossible values, no leakage), but cgpa is almost perfectly normal and capped at 4, which suggests the dataset is simulated, and the signal is weak. primary_use_case = "No AI use" is the same 148 rows as primary_ai_tool = "No AI tool", so it is dropped from the “all covariates” models.

1.2 The target: OLS on all 1200 students

fit_s <- lm(critical_thinking_score ~ ai_hours_per_week, data = data)
fit_g <- lm(cgpa ~ ai_hours_per_week, data = data)
kable(rbind(score = c(coef(fit_s)[2], confint(fit_s)[2, ], R2 = summary(fit_s)$r.squared),
            cgpa  = c(coef(fit_g)[2], confint(fit_g)[2, ], R2 = summary(fit_g)$r.squared)),
      digits = 4, col.names = c("beta(ai_hours)", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R2"))
beta(ai_hours) 2.5% 97.5% R2
score -0.3005 -0.4407 -0.1603 0.0145
cgpa 0.0079 0.0032 0.0125 0.0092

One more hour of AI use per week goes with about 0.3 points lower critical-thinking score, and a very small positive change in CGPA. Both effects explain only 1-2% of the variance.

2 LLM predictions (the AI prior)

llm_prior_labels.R splits the students with a fixed seed into 300 labelled (“known”) rows and 900 AI rows whose outcomes are hidden. For every AI row it asks an LLM (gpt-oss-20b on Groq) for a probability distribution over 8 CGPA bins and 10 score bins, given the student’s features only. This needs an API key, so it is not re-run here:

# needs GROQ_API_KEY in ~/.Renviron; resumes from the cache if interrupted
source("regression/llm_prior_labels.R")

One saved answer (students are matched back by their id, not by position):

split <- readRDS(file.path(LLM, "llm_split_v2.rds"))
resp  <- readRDS(file.path(LLM, "llm_responses_v2.rds"))

2.1 How good are the LLM predictions?

The true outcomes of the AI rows are used only here, to evaluate the LLM.

probs <- readRDS(file.path(LLM, "llm_probs_v2.rds"))
truth <- data[match(probs$student_id, data$student_id), ]
llm_quality <- function(pr, tr) data.frame(
  outcome   = c("critical_thinking_score", "cgpa"),
  mean_llm  = c(mean(pr$exp_score), mean(pr$exp_cgpa)),
  mean_true = c(mean(tr$critical_thinking_score), mean(tr$cgpa)),
  cor       = c(cor(pr$exp_score, tr$critical_thinking_score), cor(pr$exp_cgpa, tr$cgpa)),
  slope_llm  = c(coef(lm(pr$exp_score ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2], coef(lm(pr$exp_cgpa ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2]),
  slope_true = c(coef(lm(tr$critical_thinking_score ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2], coef(lm(tr$cgpa ~ tr$ai_hours_per_week))[2]))
kable(llm_quality(probs, truth), digits = 3)
outcome mean_llm mean_true cor slope_llm slope_true
critical_thinking_score 71.526 61.789 -0.029 0.332 -0.295
cgpa 3.190 3.048 -0.010 0.022 0.008 
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(truth$critical_thinking_score, probs$exp_score, pch = 16, col = "#0000ff40",
     xlab = "true score", ylab = "LLM expected score", main = "critical thinking"); abline(0, 1, col = 2)
plot(truth$cgpa, probs$exp_cgpa, pch = 16, col = "#0000ff40",
     xlab = "true CGPA", ylab = "LLM expected CGPA", main = "CGPA"); abline(0, 1, col = 2)

The LLM is too optimistic and its predictions are essentially uncorrelated with the truth. Most importantly, its implied effect of AI hours on critical thinking has the opposite sign to the data.

3 Method

Setting. We have \(n\) labelled students \((Y_i, X_i)\) and \(m\) unlabelled students \(X^*_j\) for which the LLM gives a predictive distribution \(f_{AI}(Y \mid X^*_j)\). The parameter of interest is the regression coefficient of ai_hours_per_week, defined as the minimiser of the squared-error loss.

AI prior (paper, Section 3.2). A Dirichlet process prior \(F \sim DP(\alpha, F_{AI})\) on the data-generating distribution, whose base measure \(F_{AI}\) is “features of the unlabelled students, labels drawn from the LLM”. The concentration \(\alpha\) is the prior strength: the prior is worth \(\alpha\) data points. \(\alpha = 0\) uses only the real data; \(\alpha = m\) treats every AI row like a real one (what the first draft did).

Posterior bootstrap (paper, Algorithm 1). For \(t = 1, \dots, B\): draw fake rows from \(F_{AI}\), draw weights \((w_{1:n}, w^*_{1:m}) \sim \text{Dir}(1, \dots, 1, \alpha/m, \dots, \alpha/m)\), and compute the weighted least-squares fit. The \(B\) fitted coefficients are draws from the posterior.

A minimal version for score ~ ai_hours with the 300 known students:

set.seed(30175)
X  <- cbind(1, data$ai_hours_per_week); y <- data$critical_thinking_score
kn <- match(split$known_ids, data$student_id)            # 300 labelled rows
ai <- match(split$ai_ids, data$student_id)               # 900 AI rows
P  <- as.matrix(probs[paste0("p_score_", 1:10)])         # LLM distribution per AI row
lo <- seq(0, 90, 10)

posterior_bootstrap <- function(alpha, B = 1000, m = length(ai)) {
  replicate(B, {
    w  <- rgamma(length(kn), 1)                          # Dirichlet(1,...,1) for real rows
    s  <- sample(length(ai), m, replace = TRUE)          # X* from the unlabelled students
    ys <- lo[apply(P[s, ], 1, function(p) sample(10, 1, prob = p))] + runif(m, 0, 10)  # Y* ~ LLM
    ws <- if (alpha > 0) rgamma(m, alpha / m) else rep(0, m)                           # Dir(alpha/m)
    Xa <- rbind(X[kn, ], X[ai[s], ]); ya <- c(y[kn], ys); wa <- c(w, ws)
    solve(crossprod(Xa, Xa * wa), crossprod(Xa, ya * wa))[2]
  })
}
alphas <- c(0, 30, 300, 900)
draws  <- lapply(alphas, posterior_bootstrap)
plot(NA, xlim = range(unlist(draws)), ylim = c(0, 9), xlab = "beta(ai_hours) on critical thinking",
     ylab = "posterior density", main = "Posterior bootstrap, n = 300 known students")
for (k in seq_along(alphas)) lines(density(draws[[k]]), col = k, lwd = 2)
abline(v = coef(fit_s)[2], lty = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste("alpha =", alphas), "OLS on all 1200"), col = c(seq_along(alphas), 1),
       lty = c(rep(1, length(alphas)), 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

As \(\alpha\) grows, the posterior moves from the real-data estimate towards the LLM’s (wrong) positive effect. The whole question is therefore how to choose \(\alpha\).

Choosing \(\alpha\) (paper, Section 4.1).

  • Out-of-sample: 10-fold cross-validated log predictive density on the known rows (“CV”).
  • Coverage calibration (Section 4.1.1): bootstrap the known rows, treat the known-data estimate as the truth of the bootstrap world, and take the largest \(\alpha\) whose 90% intervals still cover it at least 90% of the time (“cal”). Inside this loop the posterior-bootstrap interval is replaced by its normal approximation from the paper’s Theorem 1, which is much faster.

Comparison prior. We also fit the “power” (catalytic) AI prior of the paper’s Section 2.1, which raises the AI-row likelihood to the power \(\alpha/m\). With a normal linear model this is conjugate (closed form), and we average the AI log-likelihood over the full LLM distribution instead of using one sampled label.

Benchmark (PPI). Prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023), the method the paper compares with, estimates the coefficient as \(\hat\theta^{Y}_{L} + \lambda(\hat\theta^{f}_{U} - \hat\theta^{f}_{L})\): OLS on the real labels of the labelled students, plus the difference between OLS on the AI predictions of the unlabelled and of the labelled students. With \(\lambda = 1\) (PPI) the AI’s bias, measured on the labelled students, is removed; PPI++ tunes \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\) to minimise the variance. It needs one prediction per student (we use the mean of the LLM’s distribution), including the labelled students, which is why the v3 run also labels them.

The full implementation is regression_power_prior.R (see the Appendix). It repeats everything for both outcomes, with ai_hours only and with all covariates, with 300 and 100 known students, on the saved split and on 100 random splits (600 AI rows each; the truth is the OLS fit on all rows not used as known rows).

Sys.setenv(LLM_TAG = "v2")
source(file.path(ROOT, "regression", "regression_power_prior.R"), local = new.env())

This section uses the v2 labels (gpt-oss-20b, 15 students per request, 900 AI students). Section 5 repeats the analysis with the paper-style v3 labels, which are the main results of the report.

4.3 What the results show

  • 1:1 pooling fails. For critical thinking with 300 known students, the 90% interval covers the truth in 1% of splits and the sign is correct in 2% (real data only: 91% and 99%).
  • Choosing \(\alpha\) by CV protects the analysis. CV gives the AI rows almost no weight (mean \(\alpha\) = 1.2 for score_only), so the results are as good as with real data only, and slightly better in the models with many covariates.
  • Coverage calibration is too permissive with a biased LLM and few labels. Its bootstrap estimate of coverage follows the actual coverage closely on average (figure above), but choosing the largest acceptable \(\alpha\) often overshoots: with 100 known students the coverage drops to 72%.
  • Posterior bootstrap vs power prior. Both give almost the same estimates; the posterior bootstrap gives wider, more honest intervals when the AI weight is large.
  • Where the prior helps. For CGPA with all covariates the LLM’s (near-zero) adjusted effect is close to the truth, and the AI rows stabilise the many coefficients (RMSE 0.011 → 0.0071).

5 Second LLM run in the paper’s style (v3): main results

llm_prior_labels_v3.R repeats the elicitation in the paper’s style: one student per call, a detailed prompt that explains every feature, temperature 0.7, medium reasoning effort, and a larger model (gpt-oss-120b, served by Groq). All 900 AI students were labelled (611 through Groq’s free tier, the remaining 289 through OpenRouter routed to Groq, i.e. the same model and provider), and so were the 300 labelled students, whose predictions are needed for PPI:

Sys.setenv(LLM_PROVIDER = "openrouter")                     # paid key OPENROUTER_API_KEY, pinned to Groq
source("regression/llm_prior_labels_v3.R")                  # 900 AI students
Sys.setenv(LLM_TARGET = "known"); source("regression/llm_prior_labels_v3.R")   # 300 labelled students
Sys.setenv(LLM_TARGET = "ai", LLM_TAG = "v3"); source("regression/regression_power_prior.R")

The 100 random splits use 600 of the 900 AI students each, exactly the same splits as the v2 analysis in Section 4, so the two runs can be compared split by split. Results are in regression/output_v3/.

f_v3   <- file.path(LLM, paste0("llm_probs_", params$llm_tag_extra, ".rds"))
out_v3 <- file.path(ROOT, "regression", paste0("output_", params$llm_tag_extra))
if (!file.exists(f_v3)) {
  cat("*The", params$llm_tag_extra, "run is not finished yet; this section fills in automatically",
      "once `", basename(f_v3), "` exists.*\n")
} else {
  p3 <- readRDS(f_v3); t3 <- data[match(p3$student_id, data$student_id), ]
  p2 <- probs[match(p3$student_id, probs$student_id), ]      # v2 on the SAME students
  cat("LLM predictions vs truth: both runs evaluated on the same", nrow(p3), "AI students.\n\n")
  q  <- rbind(cbind(run = "v2 (gpt-oss-20b, 15 per call)", llm_quality(p2, t3)),
              cbind(run = paste(params$llm_tag_extra, "(paper style, gpt-oss-120b)"), llm_quality(p3, t3)))
  print(kable(q, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE))
  if (file.exists(file.path(out_v3, "replicates_summary.csv"))) {
    r3 <- read.csv(file.path(out_v3, "replicates_summary.csv"))
    r3 <- r3[r3$setting %in% names(settings) & r3$model %in% c("score_only", "cgpa_only"),
             c("model", "n_known", "setting", "mean_alpha", "mean_lambda", "rmse", "coverage", "width", "sign_ok")]
    r3$setting <- settings[r3$setting]
    cat("\n\n100 random splits with the", params$llm_tag_extra, "labels:\n\n")
    print(kable(r3, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE))
  } else {
    cat("\n\n*Run `Sys.setenv(LLM_TAG = \"", params$llm_tag_extra,
        "\"); source(\"regression/regression_power_prior.R\")` to add the 100-split results.*\n", sep = "")
  }
}

What the v3 results show (100 random splits, AI hours only):

  • The AI prior helps when the LLM’s belief points the right way. For critical thinking with 100 labelled students, 1:1 pooling reduces the RMSE from 0.293 to 0.116 and the interval width from 0.82 to 0.45, with coverage 0.98 and the correct sign in 100% of splits.
  • It fails when the LLM’s belief points the wrong way. For CGPA, 1:1 pooling covers the truth in 23% (300 labelled) and 9% (100 labelled) of splits.
  • CV is safe but cautious (mean alpha 6.4 for critical thinking, RMSE 0.274 with 100 labelled), because it judges the AI by its predictions for individual students, which are poor.
  • Coverage calibration captures the benefit but not the risk: RMSE 0.202 for critical thinking, but coverage 0.78 for CGPA (posterior bootstrap, 100 labelled).
  • The posterior bootstrap keeps more honest intervals than the power prior under heavy AI weight: coverage 0.58 vs 0.23 for CGPA with 1:1 pooling (300 labelled).
  • PPI is safe but gains nothing here. It corrects the LLM’s bias, so it stays valid for CGPA (coverage 0.88 with 100 labelled, vs 0.09 for 1:1 pooling), but it is less precise than the real data for critical thinking (RMSE 0.347 vs 0.293), because the LLM cannot predict individual students. PPI++ gives the predictions little weight (mean lambda 0.13) and reproduces the real-data results.

6 Limitations

  • The dataset is synthetic (stated in its Kaggle description), so the LLM cannot have real-world knowledge about these students and the effects should not be read as real findings.
  • The effects are weak (R² ≈ 1-2%), so the real data alone already give a wide interval.
  • The LLM prior is only as good as the LLM and the prompt: v2 and v3 imply opposite effects of AI use on critical thinking.
  • The LLM’s predictive distribution is elicited as probabilities over value ranges in one call; the paper’s view of the AI as a random label generator would suggest repeated prompting, which we did not do.
  • The posterior is centred at a biased value whenever \(\alpha > 0\) and the LLM is biased (paper, discussion after Theorem 1); the method does not correct this bias, it only limits its weight. PPI corrects it, but gains no precision when the LLM cannot predict individual students.

7 Reproducibility

  • data_check.R: about 10 s. regression_power_prior.R: about 20 min, offline.
  • llm_prior_labels.R / llm_prior_labels_v3.R: need GROQ_API_KEY; their outputs are saved in data/llm/.
  • Set rerun_analysis: true in the header to recompute the 100-split study while knitting.

8.1 regression/data_check.R

# ==========================================================================
# data_check.R -- STEP 1: is campus_ai_pulse_2026.csv fit for the
# linear-regression half of the AI-prior project (O'Hagan & Rockova 2025)?
#
# Read-only: does NOT modify bapr2.R or any data file.
# Writes plots + a summary table to ./data_check_output/
# Dependencies: base R (+ jsonlite, only for the LLM-response checks).
#
# Usage: put campus_ai_pulse_2026.csv (and optionally risposte_groq_oss20b.rds,
# data_ai_campus_complete.rds) in data/llm/, then from the project root:
#        source("regression/data_check.R")
# ==========================================================================

DATA_DIR <- Sys.getenv("CAMPUS_DATA_DIR", "data")                 # folder holding the csv
LLM_DIR  <- Sys.getenv("LLM_DIR", file.path(DATA_DIR, "llm"))     # folder holding the LLM .rds files
OUT_DIR  <- Sys.getenv("CHECK_OUT_DIR", file.path("regression", "output", "data_check"))
dir.create(OUT_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

Y_SCORE <- "critical_thinking_score"
Y_GPA   <- "cgpa"
X_KEY   <- "ai_hours_per_week"
DROPPED <- c(1, 9, 13, 14, 19:24)                 # columns removed in bapr2.R

csv_file <- file.path(DATA_DIR, "campus_ai_pulse_2026.csv")
if (!file.exists(csv_file)) stop("Dataset not found: ", normalizePath(csv_file, mustWork = FALSE),
                                 "\nSet CAMPUS_DATA_DIR or copy the csv into the project folder.")

checks <- data.frame(check = character(), result = character(),
                     problem = character(), fix = character(), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
add_check <- function(check, result, problem, fix = "") {
  checks[nrow(checks) + 1, ] <<- list(check, result, problem, fix)
  cat(sprintf("\n[%s] %s -> %s\n", problem, check, result))
}
section <- function(txt) cat("\n\n==========", txt, "==========\n")
skew <- function(x) { x <- x[!is.na(x)]; mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3 }
kurt <- function(x) { x <- x[!is.na(x)]; mean((x - mean(x))^4) / sd(x)^4 - 3 }

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
section("A. SOURCE, COLUMNS, LEAKAGE")
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
raw_chr <- read.csv(csv_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, colClasses = "character",
                    na.strings = character(0))            # untouched text, for code checks
raw     <- read.csv(csv_file, stringsAsFactors = TRUE)    # exactly as bapr2.R reads it

col_info <- data.frame(idx = seq_along(raw), name = names(raw),
                       class = sapply(raw, function(v) class(v)[1]),
                       n_unique = sapply(raw, function(v) length(unique(v))),
                       dropped_in_bapr2 = seq_along(raw) %in% DROPPED,
                       example = sapply(raw_chr, function(v) paste(head(unique(v), 3), collapse = " / ")),
                       row.names = NULL)
print(col_info, right = FALSE)
write.csv(col_info, file.path(OUT_DIR, "columns.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

for (v in c(Y_SCORE, Y_GPA, X_KEY))
  if (!v %in% names(raw)) stop("Expected column missing: ", v)
if (any(c(Y_SCORE, Y_GPA, X_KEY) %in% names(raw)[DROPPED]))
  add_check("bapr2 drop list", "drops an outcome or the key predictor!", "YES", "fix column indices")
add_check("Columns dropped by bapr2.R",
          paste(names(raw)[DROPPED], collapse = ", "), "CHECK",
          "drop by NAME, not position, and document why each is dropped")

# Leakage: how well does each column (kept or dropped) predict each outcome on its own?
leak <- do.call(rbind, lapply(setdiff(names(raw), c(Y_SCORE, Y_GPA)), function(v) {
  x <- raw[[v]]
  if (is.factor(x) && nlevels(x) > 0.5 * nrow(raw)) return(NULL)   # ID-like
  r2 <- function(y) summary(lm(raw[[y]] ~ x))$r.squared
  data.frame(column = v, dropped = v %in% names(raw)[DROPPED],
             R2_score = round(r2(Y_SCORE), 3), R2_cgpa = round(r2(Y_GPA), 3))
}))
leak <- leak[order(-pmax(leak$R2_score, leak$R2_cgpa)), ]
print(leak, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(leak, file.path(OUT_DIR, "leakage_r2.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
sus <- leak[pmax(leak$R2_score, leak$R2_cgpa) > 0.5, ]
add_check("Leakage (single-column R2 > 0.5 for an outcome)",
          if (nrow(sus)) paste(sprintf("%s%s", sus$column, ifelse(sus$dropped, "(dropped)", "(KEPT)")), collapse = ", ") else "none",
          if (any(!sus$dropped)) "YES" else if (nrow(sus)) "OK (dropped)" else "no",
          if (any(!sus$dropped)) "remove kept columns derived from the outcome" else "")
cor_outcomes <- cor(raw[[Y_SCORE]], raw[[Y_GPA]])
add_check("cor(score, cgpa)", round(cor_outcomes, 3),
          if (abs(cor_outcomes) > 0.8) "YES" else "no",
          "bapr2 already excludes the other outcome via '- cgpa' / '- critical_thinking_score'")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
data <- raw[, -DROPPED]                       # same as bapr2.R
add_check("Dimensions (raw / after drop)",
          sprintf("%d x %d / %d x %d", nrow(raw), ncol(raw), nrow(data), ncol(data)), "no")

# 3. numeric columns read as factors
num_like <- names(raw_chr)[sapply(names(raw_chr), function(v) {
  x <- trimws(raw_chr[[v]]); x <- x[x != "" & !toupper(x) %in% c("NA", "N/A", "NAN")]
  is.factor(raw[[v]]) && length(x) > 0 && mean(!is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)))) > 0.9
})]
add_check("Numeric columns wrongly read as factors", if (length(num_like)) paste(num_like, collapse = ", ") else "none",
          if (length(num_like)) "YES" else "no", "clean the bad codes, then as.numeric()")

# 4. missing / empty / sentinel codes / duplicates
na_codes <- c("", "NA", "N/A", "NAN", "NULL", "UNKNOWN", "NONE", "-", "?", "-1", "-999", "999")
miss <- sapply(raw_chr, function(v) sum(toupper(trimws(v)) %in% na_codes))
miss <- miss[miss > 0]
print(miss)
add_check("Missing / empty / sentinel codes", if (length(miss)) paste(names(miss), miss, sep = "=", collapse = ", ") else "none",
          if (length(miss)) "CHECK" else "no", "inspect; '-1'/'999' may be legitimate values")
dup_rows    <- sum(duplicated(raw))
dup_feat    <- sum(duplicated(raw[, -1]))       # ignoring the (assumed) ID column

add_check("Duplicated rows / rows dup. ignoring col 1 / dup. values in col 1",
          sprintf("%d / %d / %d", dup_rows, dup_feat, dup_id),
          if (dup_rows + dup_feat + dup_id > 0) "YES" else "no", "deduplicate before splitting")

# 5. ranges
num_cols <- names(raw)[sapply(raw, is.numeric)]
rng <- data.frame(column = num_cols,
                  min = sapply(raw[num_cols], min, na.rm = TRUE),

print(rng)
write.csv(rng, file.path(OUT_DIR, "ranges.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
bad_gpa   <- sum(raw[[Y_GPA]] < 0 | raw[[Y_GPA]] > 4, na.rm = TRUE)

add_check("Impossible values: cgpa outside 0-4 / score outside 0-100 / ai_hours <0 or >112",
          sprintf("%d / %d / %d", bad_gpa, bad_score, bad_hours),
          if (bad_gpa + bad_score + bad_hours) "YES" else "no", "remove or cap")
if ("age" %in% names(raw)) add_check("Age range", paste(range(raw$age, na.rm = TRUE), collapse = "-"),

# 6. distributions + 'synthetic fingerprints'
png(file.path(OUT_DIR, "distributions.png"), width = 1500, height = 500)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (v in c(Y_SCORE, Y_GPA, X_KEY)) {
  hist(raw[[v]], breaks = 40, main = v, xlab = v, col = "grey80", freq = FALSE)
  curve(dnorm(x, mean(raw[[v]]), sd(raw[[v]])), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
}
dev.off()
shape <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(Y_SCORE, Y_GPA, X_KEY), function(v) {
  x <- raw[[v]]
  dec <- nchar(sub("^[^.]*\\.?", "", format(x, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)))
  data.frame(variable = v, mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), skew = round(skew(x), 2),
             ex_kurt = round(kurt(x), 2), n_unique = length(unique(x)),
             max_decimals = max(dec), pct_at_min = round(100 * mean(x == min(x)), 1),
             pct_at_max = round(100 * mean(x == max(x)), 1),
             ks_normal_p = signif(suppressWarnings(ks.test(scale(x), "pnorm")$p.value), 3),
             ks_uniform_p = signif(suppressWarnings(ks.test(x, "punif", min(x), max(x))$p.value), 3))
}))
print(shape, row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(shape, file.path(OUT_DIR, "shape.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
ceil <- shape$pct_at_min > 5 | shape$pct_at_max > 5
add_check("Ceiling / floor (>5% at min or max)", paste(shape$variable[ceil], collapse = ", "),
          if (any(ceil)) "YES" else "no", "consider censored/Tobit model or a transformation")
synth <- shape$variable[shape$ks_normal_p > 0.5 | shape$ks_uniform_p > 0.5]
add_check("Suspiciously perfect normal/uniform shape (KS p > 0.5)",
          if (length(synth)) paste(synth, collapse = ", ") else "none",

# 7. rare factor levels
fac_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.factor)]
rare <- unlist(lapply(fac_cols, function(v) {
  tb <- table(data[[v]]); r <- tb[tb < 10]
  if (length(r)) paste0(v, ":", names(r), "(", r, ")") else NULL
}))
for (v in fac_cols) { cat("\n", v, ":\n"); print(table(data[[v]])) }
add_check("Rare factor levels (<10 rows) in modelling data",
          if (length(rare)) paste(rare, collapse = ", ") else "none",
          if (length(rare)) "YES" else "no", "merge rare levels; lm() on a 300-row split can fail")
hi_card <- fac_cols[sapply(data[fac_cols], nlevels) > 20]
if (length(hi_card)) add_check("High-cardinality factors (>20 levels)", paste(hi_card, collapse = ", "),

section("C. SUITABILITY FOR LINEAR REGRESSION")
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
num_d <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.numeric)]
cm <- cor(data[num_d])
print(round(cm, 2))
write.csv(round(cm, 3), file.path(OUT_DIR, "correlations.csv"))
png(file.path(OUT_DIR, "correlations.png"), width = 900, height = 900)
par(mar = c(10, 10, 2, 2))
image(1:ncol(cm), 1:ncol(cm), cm[, ncol(cm):1], zlim = c(-1, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
      col = hcl.colors(41, "Blue-Red 3"), main = "Correlations (numeric, kept columns)")
axis(1, 1:ncol(cm), colnames(cm), las = 2); axis(2, 1:ncol(cm), rev(colnames(cm)), las = 2)
